findings.where: Screens 4 and 8, the 'Drop, pipe to throat' readout and the live line under the slider
findings.what: At the opening 4 L/s through 5 cm² the readout and live line print 30.7 kPa, because ½ × 1025 × (8² − 2²) ÷ 1000 comes out as 30.749999… in JavaScript and K.fmt rounds it down, while the screen text, screen 8's 'a quarter of 30.8' and puzzles 12 and 13 all say 30.8 kPa. Round the drop with rd() before it reaches the readout and sayFor(), as the N table already does.

'Water in a plant's pipes at everyday speeds is usually well into the eddying range' has no source. The research cites no Reynolds number formula, no viscosity and no quote about plant flows, and the brief limits Re to words and a contested range. Cut it, or say only that faster, wider and thinner flows eddy.

findings.where: Screen 11: its Why?, the hint for the 50 mm pick, the red picture labels and the right answer's picture
findings.what: 'Seawater at 2 m/s is thin and fast, so it eddies', 'It eddies even in a 50 mm pipe', 'fast, thin seawater eddies' and the right answer's picture of both seawater pipes eddying are unsourced absolutes that cannot be worked out without a viscosity. The puzzle only supports a comparison, that the oil is the most likely of the three to run smooth, so word the feedback and the picture that way.

findings.where: SHOW screens 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10: the paragraph plus the live line under the picture
findings.what: Each paragraph runs 78 to 84 words, and a 17 to 37 word live line under the slider repeats much of it, so each screen shows about 100 to 120 words, over the 90-word limit. Screen 4 is the worst: 81 + 37 words, plus a caption, all after the diagram. Trim the paragraphs, or cut the live line down to the numbers that change.

'As a rule, flow is smooth below about 2000 and eddies above about 4000' makes the upper edge sound settled, but one kept source puts the transition band as high as 10 000. Say the upper edge varies too, so the contested point is taught as contested at both ends.

The switch picks the result, 'Smooth layers' or 'Eddies', directly, where the brief promised a viscosity and speed switch. The picture shows what eddies look like but not what causes them. A switch such as 'thick oil, creeping / thin seawater, fast' that drives the pattern and the band's highlight would show the cause.
'The drop grows with the speed squared. So twice the flow gives four times the drop' skips the link between them, that the speed is in step with the flow (continuity). Add that one short sentence.

The fact-check changed the explain text to 'area × the water's average speed', because real water runs faster in the middle, but the screen still says 'area × speed'. Carry 'average' onto the screen so the steps match the checked text.
'Its column stands back up, level with the first' reads as fact, and friction is not mentioned until screen 6. Add a short sentence that a real venturi gets most of the drop back, not all of it.

A cable's volt drop is in step with the current (I × R), but the venturi's drop goes with the flow squared. The breaks never says this, so the analogy can feed one of the lesson's own listed mistakes, treating the drop as in step with the flow. Add one sentence.

findings.where: practice.text, the correction factor and the orifice plate
findings.what: 'A little under 1 for a venturi' and 'it costs less, but it loses more of the drop for good' have no quote in the research, and the brief says the discharge coefficient gets no number. Either cite them or say only that the maker gives a correction factor.

findings.where: Whole lesson, compared with the brief's row 6
findings.what: The brief promised to name the Pitot tube and the sharp-edged orifice's discharge coefficient. No screen names either: the orifice plate appears only in the practice notes, and the Pitot tube appears nowhere.

The brief promised a 'still there' continuity sum on BTEC ground, but the warm-up tests ρgh from lesson 5. Continuity is then taught from scratch on screen 2, with no fast path for what Dan may already know.
'Every picture here shows seawater in a level pipe' is not true of screen 11, which shows thick oil and three plain pipes. Reword the lead so it does not claim more than the pictures show.
'The drop goes with the flow squared: twice the flow…' and 'Reynolds number: smooth below about 2000, …' chain clauses on colons. Split each into short sentences.

When the slug cycles round, it and its two arrows appear whole at the inlet and vanish at the outlet, about every 14 s at 4 L/s. On entry its back arrow starts about 37 units off the left edge, so its tail is clipped. Fade the slug in and out at the ends of the pipe.
'1025 × 3 is a mass in kilograms' is loose. It is the mass, in kg, of the column standing on each square metre, so say that.
The prediction ends 'Which is right?' without asking the real question. Ask it directly: 'How will the throat's column stand?'

findings.where: Screens 12 and 13, the closing mixed puzzles
findings.what: Both reuse the lesson's own 150 kPa and 30.8 kPa and test lesson 5's skills (absolute pressure, h = p ÷ ρg). No closing puzzle asks for continuity and Bernoulli together on fresh numbers, for example from two areas and a flow to a drop.
